headline: Scott Bessent's Treasury intervention is about capping the speed of yield rises, not pushing rates down; outcome uncertain against commodity-driven inflation
reasoning: Epstein is uncertain about the rationale for Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's intervention using the trillion-dollar Exchange Stabilization Fund. He interprets Bessent's intent as capping the rate at which yields move higher rather than actively suppressing them, hoping market forces eventually bring them back down — a theory he aligns with Fed member Williams's view that inflation is easing. However, Epstein remains unconvinced, pointing out that commodity prices, particularly oil driven by Iran, and grain prices are not cooperating with that thesis.
quote: I don't know what he's talking about and I don't know why he's doing it. First of all, I don't know that the Treasury is the people to set interest rate policies for the country. That's the first thing. He has the trillion dollar slush fund to do it. I think that what he's saying, and I think he was misconstrued, is he's going to try to cap the speed that it moves at to the upside. I don't think he's trying to push interest rates down. I think he's trying to cap them and hopes that the market forces take them back down.

headline: New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh ushering in hawkish era, using hawkish talk to avoid near-term rate hike
reasoning: Epstein sees Fed Chair Warsh as a departure from Yellen and Powell, noting the ultra-short policy statement, refusal to vote on the dot plot, and formation of five task forces as signals he is putting his own stamp on the Fed. Warsh is critiquing the Fed's backward-looking approach to data and suggesting forward-looking private sector guidance as a better model. Epstein believes the hawkish talk is strategic — designed to get markets to do the Fed's tightening work without actually raising rates in the near term, partly to pre-empt pressure from President Trump.
quote: He's putting his stamp on what the fed chair is going to look like, and he's bringing it up to today. In other words, the fed always looks at data. You hear that. But they don't look it forward at it. And that has been the big problem all the way through. They look at current data. They're not forward thinking. And this fed chair said you know, maybe there's better things to look at. Maybe we should be looking at what private companies are doing as an example, on earnings period every quarter when they come out. Most of the companies not all, but most, give you forward guidance... I think the whole speech he gave today was centered on a hawkish talk to get the market to do his job without him having to raise interest rates in the near term.
